reason: Build the peripheral nerve route first by adding Schwann cells to the sensory and motor fibres.
expectation: I expect a peripheral nerve with Schwann cells wrapping its axons, though the exact result is uncertain.

alternatives.reason: Building the spinal cord also supports the routes, but I chose to start at the periphery.

effect: The peripheral nerve now has wrapped axons carrying signals in both directions; the central routes still need building.
reaction: The gaps in the wrapping are visible, though their role is not explained.
reason: Build the spinal route next, connecting the peripheral nerve's destination to central grey matter.
expectation: I expect a spinal cord structure combining central grey matter with longitudinal tracts.

alternatives.reason: The brain also needs its white matter connected, but the spinal cord comes first along the peripheral route.

effect: The spinal cord now provides a central structure to connect with the peripheral nerve.
reaction: The butterfly-shaped grey matter makes the cord's arrangement clear.
reason: Connect the peripheral nerve to the spinal cord to build the route inward.
expectation: I expect a connected peripheral nerve and spinal cord, with sensory and motor paths represented.

alternatives.reason: The brain also needs building, but I want to connect the spinal route first.

effect: The peripheral nerve now connects sensory entry and motor exit at the spinal cord, with local circuits between them.
reaction: The separate entry and exit paths clarify how the shared nerve connects to the cord.
reason: Build the brain so the sensory route can eventually reach its destination.
expectation: I expect a brain structure combining grey matter and connecting white matter.

alternatives.reason: Pain input could trace a spinal response now, but the brain is also needed for the sensory goal.

effect: The brain and its long central pathways are built, ready to connect to the spinal cord.
reaction: The cutaway distinguishes the cerebral grey and white matter, though the pathway details remain unclear.
reason: Connect the brain and spinal cord to complete the central route for sensory information.
expectation: I expect a connected brain and spinal cord with ascending and descending pathways; the exact result is uncertain.

alternatives.reason: Pain input could explore the spinal route, but connecting the brain first supports the sensory goal.

effect: The brain, spinal cord and peripheral routes now form a connected model ready for tracing signals.
reaction: The connection brings the separate structures together, although the small arrows leave the detailed routes to explore.
reason: Trace touch from the periphery toward the brain to address the sensory goal.
expectation: I expect a sensory pathway from the fingertip through the spinal cord toward the brain, though its exact stations are uncertain.

alternatives.reason: Pain could also trace sensory input and potentially lead to a spinal response, but I chose touch first.
Cortical motor activity could explore the outgoing route, but I want to trace sensation first.

effect: Touch activity reached the cortex via the cord, brainstem and a deep relay, completing the sensory goal.
reaction: The route is clear, though the relay is not named.
reason: Trace pain input to explore the spinal route to an outgoing motor signal.
expectation: I expect pain input to engage a spinal circuit and possibly produce an outgoing motor signal; the details are uncertain.

alternatives.reason: Cortical motor activity offers the other route, but the spinal circuit is the shorter path to explore.

effect: The pain input produced a coordinated spinal motor output, completing the motor goal without requiring a cortical route.
reaction: The active and quiet motor axons make the local circuit's opposing effects clear.

mostWorthwhile.text: Tracing pain into the spinal circuit was most worthwhile: it connected excitation and inhibition to coordinated motor output and showed that a response can begin before conscious perception.

leastWorthwhile.text: The brain construction was relatively static; its cutaway identified regions but left the pathway details unclear until the later sensory trace.

surprise.text: The spinal circuit could activate one motor group while inhibiting its opponent, without waiting for conscious perception.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless, although the gaps in the peripheral nerve's wrapping were shown without explaining their role.

continue.text: I would continue to see how the cortical motor route compares with the spinal route, which was left unexplored when the chapter ended.
